title: The Over-Soul
hookLine: he wrote of a great soul in which each person's life is contained (The Over-Soul)

lines: A SPRING OUT OF THE ROCK.
A STREAM WHOSE SOURCE IS HIDDEN.
cards: A spring comes up out of a hillside. Clear water, out of the dark, out of rock, from somewhere nobody can point to.
Follow it downhill and it becomes a stream, then joins other streams, and somewhere far below it is a river. The water at the spring has no idea about the river.

Near the start of one of his essays, Emerson turns that picture on us: "Man is a stream whose source is hidden." Our lives, he says, descend into us from somewhere we can't see. The essay is called The Over-Soul.

teach.b: First, the problem. "We live in succession, in division, in parts, in particles." That's ordinary life: one thing after another, me over here, you over there, a day chopped into tasks, a self chopped into roles.
Second, what he says is underneath.
Within each person, Emerson writes, is the soul of the whole, the wise silence, the universal beauty to which every part is equally related.

He calls it the Over-Soul: a unity within which each person's particular life is contained, and made one with all the others. Not a soul floating somewhere above us. A larger life we're each already inside.
Third, how he says we notice it. Not by argument, but in moments: a conversation where two people suddenly understand more than either brought to it, a sudden insight, the quiet behind thought.
He calls it a common heart. In his picture, the little self, with its worries and its name, sits inside something much larger. Fourth, why this changes the week.
Trust thyself and insist on yourself could sound like a lonely road.
The Over-Soul is the other half: the self Emerson trusts is a door into what everyone shares.
That's why self-reliance, read carefully, opens out rather than closing in. Some readers hear echoes of older traditions here. Emerson's reading from India gets its own day later in this block.

how: Some readers of Emerson's The Over-Soul take it as an invitation to notice the larger life they share with others, in moments of insight, quiet, or real conversation.

games.why: The Over-Soul: the self he trusts is a door into what everyone shares, the soul of the whole.

practice: Notice the edges you usually live inside, this body, this name, today's list, then let your attention widen: the room, the people in the building or the street, the city, the weather moving over it.
The breath you're taking was outside you a moment ago and will be again. Let the edges soften a little, and rest as one stream in a much larger river.
